title: The search for dark matter takes a tantalizing turn, but one Northeast Ohio scientist has questions
byline: Ideastream Public Media | By Jeff St. Clair
excerpt: There's potential new proof of the existence of dark matter, the mysterious particle that could explain the long-observed motion of galaxies.
content:
Published September 18, 2026 at 1:34 PM EDT

A specially built detector buried in a South Dakota gold mine has provided the first potential interaction with dark matter — a mysterious particle that’s key to our understanding of the universe.

Dark matter is believed to make up 85% of all matter but has never been directly detected.

The LZ, or LUX-ZEPLIN, experiment under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy has recently provided tantalizing evidence for the existence of a dark matter particle.

Spokesperson Richard Gaitskell of Brown University said statistically there is a 1 in 200 chance the newly released finding is just background noise.

“We have one event that does not appear to be explainable with our current understanding of background (noise),” he said.

Gaitskell has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years.

“This is the first time anybody has suggested evidence for the type of signal we’re seeing,” Gaitskell said.

He cautioned it's only one event, but added, “we are very excited about this opportunity.”

The LZ detector includes a chamber filled with 10 tons of purified liquid xenon surrounded by an array of light sensors, plus other equipment to reduce background interference.

When a proposed particle of dark matter, known as a WIMP, or Weakly Interacting Massive Particle, strikes a xenon nucleus, an electron and flash of light are emitted creating signals in the detector.

Gaitskell says his team spent nearly a year analyzing the data, collected in 2023, before releasing their findings to the public.

“We only decided to share this with the wider scientific community after doing a major additional review ourselves to see whether we felt we understood the behavior of the detector well enough,” he said.

The signal was discovered on a second review of the data because it appeared in a region that hadn’t initially been thought to include the sort of WIMPs they were looking for.

“For this new analysis we decided we would use a broader set of possible interactions between the dark matter and the xenon nuclei,” said Gaitskell.

In physics terms, he said, “you might call it the next leading order of interactions.”

But he says the finding does fall within the range of signals that could be dark matter.

“Theorists going back 15 years have been looking at this type of interaction,” said Gaitskell.

Why does ‘dark matter’ matter?

The idea of dark matter dates back to the 1930’s when scientists first began measuring the motion of distant galaxies.

Early observers, like Swiss-born astronomer Fritz Zwicky, who coined the term, found that these groups of stars moved in ways that suggested their mass was much greater than expected.

Later in the 1970’s, dark matter was used to explain the rotation rates of spiral galaxies. There must be some invisible material that provides the gravity necessary to hold them together at the edges.

Data from today’s high-powered telescopes have added to the now well-accepted idea that around 85% of the matter in the universe is dark matter, which can’t be seen or directly detected, but helps explain the motion of galazies.

But there are other theories that don’t include dark matter.

One of them is called MOND, or Modified Newtonian Dynamics.

Astronomer Stacy McGaugh at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland is one of its proponents.

Instead of adding an unexplained particle to provide the extra gravity, MOND tweaks Newton’s laws of motion at the edges of galaxies to explain why they rotate faster than expected, McGaugh said.

“Just a tiny acceleration, ridiculously small, and yet that is the centripetal acceleration holding stars in their orbits around galaxies,” said McGaugh.

After analyzing the motion of hundreds of galaxies, McGaugh and other dark matter skeptics, said MOND better describes the complex interactions of gravity.

“The scientific method says we should give preference to the theory whose predictions come true and for galaxy dynamics that’s modified Newtonian dynamics not dark matter,” McGaugh said.

But why is MOND not the prevailing view?

McGaugh said dark matter sounds less crazy to most scientists than changing the laws of gravity.

Either way, he said, “clearly we have fundamental things left to learn about how the universe works.”
